resources.string: All app traffic runs through the local VPN and is forwarded unchanged. DNS-over-TLS (port 853) is blocked so that automatic Private DNS falls back to readable DNS.

Bytes per second, sent and received, over the selected window. One axis: height is the rate, the baseline is zero, and the top label marks the peak.

Each band is one direction of traffic. A tall received band with a thin sent band is a download (video, a web page); the reverse is an upload. Short spikes are bursts; a steady plateau is a stream. The two series share one scale so their heights are directly comparable — there is deliberately no second axis.
Share of traffic volume by protocol, largest first; smaller protocols are folded into “Other”. Read each segment’s width as its fraction of all bytes.

TLS and QUIC are encrypted web traffic (QUIC is HTTP/3 over UDP); plain HTTP and DNS are readable. A large plain-HTTP or DNS slice is worth a look — that traffic is in the clear. The bar is weighted by bytes, so one heavy download can dominate it; the legend also gives each protocol’s connection count.
Share of the connections shown below, by protocol. Weighted by connection count, not bytes, so it reflects the list — it follows the search and filters.
No packets of this connection in the capture buffer.
TLS and QUIC payloads are encrypted: the decoded view shows the handshake and marks application data as encrypted.
Start capture when the phone starts
Needs the VPN permission, which you grant the first time you start a capture in the app.
On: Android may stop the capture while the app is in the background.
Off: the capture can keep running in the background.
On: Android starts the capture after a reboot and restarts it if it stops.
Android starts the capture after a reboot and restarts it if it stops. Tap the gear next to Traffic AL and turn on Always-on VPN.
Huawei: Settings → Battery → App launch → Traffic AL → Manage manually, with all three switches on, or EMUI stops the capture.
Encrypted PCAPNG files with the app of each packet, in the app\'s private storage. Export them under Recordings.
When the recordings reach the limit, the oldest packets are deleted.
Recordings and exports carry the TLS keys for the sessions in them, so Wireshark shows that traffic decrypted. The keys stay inside the exported file.
The app never derives keys. It reads a key log you place at %1$s — from your own app built with SSLKEYLOGFILE, or a key log written with root. Pinned apps stay opaque. See docs/DECRYPTION.md.
Traffic AL %1$s · GPL-3.0-or-later. No analytics: captured data stays on the phone unless you export it.
Saving to storage is off (Settings → Recording).

Loaded from a recording. Protocol and category labels are added by live analysis and aren\'t saved; connections show their server name instead.

Updates while open; reads your key log live.
No readable HTTP traffic yet. Start a capture and use your apps.
No TLS keys placed, so encrypted traffic can\'t be read. Add a key log (Settings → TLS decryption) to see inside HTTPS and QUIC.
Encrypted — no keys for this connection (or the app pins its certificate).
Share of your web traffic, by volume, that could be read versus what stayed encrypted (no keys, or the app pins its certificate).

“Readable” is plaintext HTTP plus TLS/QUIC decrypted with your own keys; “Encrypted” is everything no key could open. Routing an app through your mitmproxy moves it from encrypted to readable; a pinned app stays encrypted by design. A large encrypted share is not a problem in itself — it means that traffic is private even from you.
%1$d apps fully readable · %2$d opaque (pinned or no keys)

Route your apps through mitmproxy to read more. Run mitmproxy on your computer, install its CA (tools/decryption/system-ca.sh), and point its SSLKEYLOGFILE at Traffic AL\'s key-log path (Settings → TLS decryption). Applies when you next start the capture. Pinned apps and QUIC stay opaque.
Too many wrong PINs. Try again in %1$d s.
Without the PIN the app can only be opened again by erasing all recordings and the connection history. This also removes the app lock.
Ask for a PIN when the app opens and after a minute in the background. The capture keeps running while the app is locked. Screenshots of the app are blocked.
No fingerprint is set up on this phone.
Recordings and the connection history are encrypted with keys protected by the Android Keystore, which never hands them out. Exported files are not encrypted.
Deletes all recordings and the connection history.
All recordings and the connection history are deleted. This cannot be undone.
Exported %1$d packets (%2$s). %3$d file(s) ended early, e.g. because the system stopped the capture while writing; they are included up to that point.
The connections and DNS lookups shown in the app are deleted, also those saved from earlier captures. Recordings stay.
